<poem>{{smaller block|With marble greet ygrounde and myxt with lyme
Polisshe alle ''uppe'' thy werke in goodly time.
{{right|''Palladius'', Husbondrie (E. E. T. S.), p. 15.}}}}</poem>
{{smaller block|He’ll win ''up'' all the money in the town.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Alchemist, i. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|The Indians killed ''up'' all their own swine, so as Capt. Lovell had none. ''Winthrop'', Hist. New England, I. 466.}}

'''13.''' To or at an end; over: specifically, in Great Britain, noting adjournment or dissolution: as, Parliament is ''up''.
<poem>{{smaller block|When the tyme was ourtyrnyt, and the tru ''vp'',
Agamynon the grekys gedrit in the fild.
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 7207.}}}}</poem>
{{smaller block|That shall be according as you are in the Mind after your Month is ''up''.
{{right|''N. Bailey'', tr. of Colloquies of Erasmus, I. 446.}}}}
{{smaller block|The court is ''up''—i. e., it does not now sit.
{{right|''N. and Q.'', 7th ser., VI. 11.}}}}

'''14†.''' Open.
{{smaller block|His door is ''uppe''.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Canterbury Tales (F), l. 615 (ed. Skeat).}}}}
{{smaller block|[''Up'' is often used elliptically for ''go up'', ''come up'', ''rise up'', ''stand up'', ''speak up'', and similar phrases in which the verb is omitted; and with ''with'' following, it has the effect of a transitive verb. In provincial or vulgar speech the adverb so used is sometimes inflected as a verb.}}
{{smaller block|I will ''up'', saith the Lord. {{right|Ps. xii. 6 (Psalter).}}}}
{{smaller block|''Up'' with my tent there! here will I lie to-night!
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., v. 3. 7.}}}}
<poem>{{smaller block|The true-bred gamester ''ups'' afresh, and then
Falls to’t again. ''Quarles'', Emblems, ii. 14.}}</poem>
{{smaller block|She ''up'' with her pattens, and beat out their brains.
{{right|''The Farmer’s Old Wife'' (Child’s Ballads, VIII. 258).}}}}
{{smaller block|So saying, she ''ups'' with her brawny arm, and gave Susy such a douse on the side of her head as left her fast asleep for an hour and upward. ''Brooke'', Fool of Quality, I. 134.]}}

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|up|6658|upas}}</noinclude>{{smaller block|there was a rap at his front door, we should know that he was not ''up'' to his work.
{{right|''W. K. Clifford'', Lectures, II. 137.}}}}
'''7.''' In or into activity, motion, operation, etc. Specifically—(''a'') Out of bed; risen from sleep.
{{smaller block|<poem>Fair day, my lords. You are all larkes this morning,
''Vp'' with the sun: you are stirring earely.</poem>
{{right|''Heywood'', If you Know not me, ii.}}}}
{{smaller block|''May.'' Where is your mistress, villain? when went she abroad?
''Pren.'' Abroad, sir! why, as soon as she was ''up'', sir.
{{right|''Dekker and Webster'', Northward Ho, i. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|It was late, it is true, but on a May evening even country people keep ''up'' till eight or nine o’clock.
{{right|''Mrs. Gaskell'', Sylvia’s Lovers, xix.}}}}
(''b'') In commotion, tumult, or revolt; roused: as, to have one’s temper ''up;'' to be ''up'' in arms.
{{smaller block|<poem>’Tis treason to be ''up'' against the King.</poem>
{{right|''Marlowe'', Edward II., i. 4.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>[''Within.''] Liberty, liberty!
''Duke.'' What, is the city ''up?''
''Boats.'' They are ''up'' and glorious,
And rolling like a storm they come.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Double Marriage, v. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Now my anger ’s ''up'',
Ten thousand virgins kneeling at my feet,
And with one general cry howling for mercy,
Shall not redeem thee.</poem>
{{right|''Massinger'', Unnatural Combat, ii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Till ''up'' in Arms my Passions rose,
And cast away her Yoke.</poem>
{{right|''Cowley'', The Chronicle, st. 3.}}}}
(''c'') In process of occurrence or performance; in progress: as, what is ''up?''
{{smaller block|The hunt is ''up''.
{{right|''Shak.'', Tit. And., ii. 2. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The woodland rings with laugh and shout,
As if a hunt were ''up''.</poem>
{{right|''Bryant'', Song of Marion’s Men.}}}}

{{smaller block|I’ll finish my cigar in the betting-room, and hear what ’s up.
{{right|''Jeaffreson'', Live it Down, xxiv.}}}}

{{smaller block|(''d'') In or into activity, operation, or use; at work; on; going.}}

<poem>Loud is the vale, the voice is ''up''
With which she speaks when storms are gone.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Wordsworth'', At Grasmere after a Storm.}}}}

{{smaller block|It will suffice just to name the meteorologic processes eventually set ''up'' in the Earth’s atmosphere.
{{right|''H. Spencer'', First Principles, § 151.}}}}

{{smaller block|The Harriet Lane, not having steam ''up'', could not draw near the scene of action, and confined herself to firing in the direction of the bridge.
{{right|''Comte de Paris'', Civil War in America (trans.), II. 639.}}}}

{{smaller block|(''e'') In or into prominence or consideration; into or to the light: as, a missing article turns ''up''; a question comes ''up'' for discussion; to bring ''up'' a new topic of conversation.}}

{{smaller block|How dangerous it was to bring ''up'' an ill report upon this good land, which God had found out and given to his people.
{{right|''Winthrop'', Hist. New England, I. 400.}}}}

{{smaller block|His name was ''up'' through all the adjoining Provinces, eev’n to Italy and Rome.
{{right|''Milton'', Hist. Eng., ii.}}}}

{{smaller block|Whether it be possible for him, from his own imagination, to . . . raise ''up'' to himself the idea of that particular shade [previously unknown].
{{right|''Hume'', Human Understanding, ii.}}}}

'''8.''' Onward to or from a specified time: as, an account ''up'' to date.

<poem>We were tried friends: I from childhood ''up''
Had known him.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Wordsworth'', Excursion, i.}}}}

{{smaller block|All men knew what the conduct of James had been ''up'' to that very time.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Hist. Eng., vii.}}}}

'''9.''' To complete existence, maturity, or age: as, to spring or grow ''up''; to bring ''up'' a child properly.

{{smaller block|And so he dide, and put his owne sone, whiche was not fully of half yere age, to be norisshed ''vp'' with a-nother woman. {{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), i. 112.}}}}
{{smaller block|Train ''up'' a child in the way he should go. {{right|Prov. xxii. 6.}}}}
'''10.''' In or into a place of storage, retirement, concealment, etc., as for safe-keeping or as not being used or required at the time; aside; by: as, to put ''up'' one’s work for an hour or two; to put ''up'' medicine in a bottle.
{{smaller block|Lay not ''up'' for yourselves treasures upon earth. {{right|Mat. vi. 19.}}}}
{{smaller block|Keep ''up'' your bright swords, for the dew will rust them. {{right|''Shak.'', Othello, i. 2. 59.}}}}
{{smaller block|Those highly-compounded nitrogenous molecules in which so much motion is locked ''up''. {{right|''H. Spencer'', First Principles, § 104.}}}}
'''11.''' In or into a state of union, contraction, closeness of parts, etc.: together; close: as, to fold ''up'' a letter; to shrivel ''up;'' to draw ''up'' cloth upon a gathering-thread; to shut ''up'' an umbrella; to add ''up'' a column of figures.
{{smaller block|<poem>She starts, like one that spies an adder
Wreathed ''up'' in fatal folds just in his way.</poem>{{right|''Shak.'', Venus and Adonis, l. 878.}}}}
{{smaller block|To sum ''up'' the matter, a study of the statistics reveals the fact that no absolute participle occurs in Anglo-Saxon without having a prototype in Latin, either directly or indirectly. {{right|''Amer. Jour. Philol.'', X. 344.}}}}
'''12.''' To the required, desired, or uttermost point; to completion or fulfilment; wholly; thoroughly; quite: as, to pay ''up'' one’s debts; to burn ''up'' the fuel; to build ''up'' one’s constitution; to use ''up'' one’s patience.
<poem>{{smaller block|With marble greet ygrounde and myxt with lyme
Polisshe alle ''uppe'' thy werke in goodly time.
{{right|''Palladius'', Husbondrie (E. E. T. S.), p. 15.}}}}</poem>
{{smaller block|He’ll win ''up'' all the money in the town.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Alchemist, i. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|The Indians killed ''up'' all their own swine, so as Capt. Lovell had none. ''Winthrop'', Hist. New England, I. 466.}}

'''13.''' To or at an end; over: specifically, in Great Britain, noting adjournment or dissolution: as, Parliament is ''up''.
<poem>{{smaller block|When the tyme was ourtyrnyt, and the tru ''vp'',
Agamynon the grekys gedrit in the fild.
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 7207.}}}}</poem>
{{smaller block|That shall be according as you are in the Mind after your Month is ''up''.
{{right|''N. Bailey'', tr. of Colloquies of Erasmus, I. 446.}}}}
{{smaller block|The court is ''up''—i. e., it does not now sit.
{{right|''N. and Q.'', 7th ser., VI. 11.}}}}

'''14†.''' Open.
{{smaller block|His door is ''uppe''.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Canterbury Tales (F), l. 615 (ed. Skeat).}}}}
{{smaller block|[''Up'' is often used elliptically for ''go up'', ''come up'', ''rise up'', ''stand up'', ''speak up'', and similar phrases in which the verb is omitted; and with ''with'' following, it has the effect of a transitive verb. In provincial or vulgar speech the adverb so used is sometimes inflected as a verb.}}
{{smaller block|I will ''up'', saith the Lord. {{right|Ps. xii. 6 (Psalter).}}}}
{{smaller block|''Up'' with my tent there! here will I lie to-night!
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., v. 3. 7.}}}}
<poem>{{smaller block|The true-bred gamester ''ups'' afresh, and then
Falls to’t again. ''Quarles'', Emblems, ii. 14.}}</poem>
{{smaller block|She ''up'' with her pattens, and beat out their brains.
{{right|''The Farmer’s Old Wife'' (Child’s Ballads, VIII. 258).}}}}
{{smaller block|So saying, she ''ups'' with her brawny arm, and gave Susy such a douse on the side of her head as left her fast asleep for an hour and upward. ''Brooke'', Fool of Quality, I. 134.]}}

'''All up with.''' See ''all.''

{{smaller block|I saw that it was ''all up with'' our animals. Weak as I was myself, I was obliged to walk, as my ox could not carry me up the steep inclination.
{{right|''Sir S. W. Baker'', Heart of Africa, p. 259.}}}}

'''Hard up.''' See ''hard, adv.''—'''To back, ball, bear up.''' See the verbs.—'''To bear up''' or '''put up the helm,''' to move the tiller toward the upper or windward side of a vessel.

{{smaller block|Captaine Ratliffe (Captaine of the Pinnace) rather desired to ''beare vp the helme'' to returne for England then make further search.
{{right|Quoted in ''Capt. John Smith’s'' True Travels, I. 150.}}}}

'''To beat, blow, bring, come, cut, do, draw, fire, flush, get, give,''' etc., '''up.''' See the verbs.—'''To have up,''' to bring before a magistrate or court of justice.

{{smaller block|I’ll ''have'' you ''up'' for assault.
{{right|''Farrar.''}}}}

'''To hitch, hold, hush up.''' See the verbs.—'''To look up,''' to improve in health, value, etc.: as, the property seems to be ''looking up.'' See also ''look''<sup>1</sup>, ''v. t.'' [Colloq.]—'''To make, pull, put, tear,''' etc., '''up.''' See the verbs.—'''To up stick,''' to pack up; make ready to go away. [Slang.]

{{smaller block|I followed the cattle-tracks till I came to the great Billebong where they were fishing; and I made them ''up stick'' and take me home.
{{right|''H. Kingsley'', Hillyars and Burtons, xxviii.}}}}

'''Up and down.''' (''a'') In a vertical position or direction; upright: in nautical use said of the chain when the ship is directly over the anchor. (''b'') Here and there; to and fro; back and forth; one way and another.

<poem>But hit was kept alway with a dragoun,
And many other merveils, ''up and doun.''</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Chaucer'', Good Women, l. 1431.}}}}

{{smaller block|And the Lord said unto Satan: From whence comest thou? And Satan . . . said: From going to and fro in the earth, and from walking ''up and down'' in it.
{{right|Job ii. 2.}}}}

{{smaller block|There are some Sycophants here that idolize him [the Cardinal], and I blush to hear what profane Hyperboles are printed ''up and down'' of him. {{right|''Howell'', Letters, I. vi. 44.}}

Mem. Lloyd had, about the beginning of the civill warres, a MS. of this Saint’s concerning Chymistrey, and sayes that there are severall MSS. of his ''up and downe'' in England. {{right|''Aubrey'', Lives (Saint Dunstan).}}}}

(''c''†) In every particular; completely; wholly; exactly; just.

{{smaller block|He [Phocion] was euen Socrates ''vp and downe'' in this pointe and behalfe, that no man euer sawe hym either laughe or weepe. {{right|''Udall'', tr. of Apophthegms of Erasmus, p. 324. (''Davies.'')}}

The mother’s mouth ''up and down, up and down.'' {{right|''Middleton'', Chaste Maid, iii. 2.}}}}

(''d'') Downright; bluntly; without mincing matters; “without gloves”: as, to handle a matter ''up and down;'' to talk ''up and down:'' sometimes used adjectively: as, to be ''up and down'' with a person. [Colloq.]

{{smaller block|Talk about coddling! it ’s little we get o’ that, the way the Lord fixes things in this world, dear knows. He ’s pretty ''up and down'' with us, by all they tell us. You must take things right off, when they’re goin’. Ef you don’t, so much the worse for you; they won’t wait for you. {{right|''H. B. Stowe'', Oldtown, p. 240.}}}}

'''Up to.''' (''a'') As high as; as far advanced as; equal to. See defs. 4, 5, 6. (''b'') On the point of doing; about to do; planning; engaged in. [Colloq.]

{{smaller block|“Wot are you ''up to'', old feller?” asked Mr. Bailey, with . . . graceful rakishness. He was quite the man-about-town of the conversation. {{right|''Dickens'', Martin Chuzzlewit, xxvi.}}

“Here you are, you little minx,” said Miss Asphyxia. “What are you ''up to'' now? Come, the waggin’s waiting.” {{right|''H. B. Stowe'', Oldtown, p. 124.}}

Then he [King James II.] signified me to kneel, which I did, . . . and then he gave me a little tap very nicely}} upon my shoulder before I knew what he was ''up to'', and said, “Arise, Sir John Ridd!”
{{right|''R. D. Blackmore'', Lorna Doone, lxviii.}}}}

{{smaller|'''Up to snuff, to the ears, to the elbows, to the hilt.''' See ''snuff''<sup>1</sup>, ''ear''<sup>1</sup>, etc.—'''Up to the knocker, up to the door,''' reaching the desired standard; good; excellent. [Slang.]}}

'''II.''' ''prep.'' '''1.''' Upward or aloft in or on; to, toward, near, or at the top of: as, to climb ''up'' a tree.
{{smaller block|The wedercoc thet is ''ope'' the steple.
{{right|''Ayenbite of Inwyt'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 180.}}
As you go ''up'' the stairs into the lobby.
{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, iv. 3. 39.}}
<poem>A voice replied, far ''up'' the height,
Excelsior! ''Longfellow'', Excelsior.</poem>
<poem>Elaine, the lily maid of Astolat,
High in her chamber ''up'' a tower to the east
Guarded the sacred shield of Lancelot.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Lancelot and Elaine.}}}}
'''2.''' To, toward, or at the source, head, center, or important part of: as, to walk ''up'' town; often, toward the interior of (a region): as, the explorers went ''up'' country.
{{smaller block|''Up'' Fish Street! down Saint Magnus’ Corner!
{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. VI., iv. 8. 1.}}
The author put off at dawn, from a French ship of war, in a small boat with a handful of men, to row ''up'' a river on the coast of Anam. ''Fortnightly Rev.'', N. S., XLIII. 656.

The man who abandoned a farm ''up'' the Hudson, which had been in the family for generations, and came to New York without having any particular vocation in view, . . . was a type of a large class. ''The Century'', XL. 634.}}
'''3†.''' Upon or on (in many senses).
{{smaller block|A glose ''ope'' the sautere.
{{right|''Ayenbite of Inwyt'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 187.}}}}

{{smaller block|Helpes hastily hende men i hote, ''vp'' ȝour liues!
{{right|''William of Palerne'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 2378.}}
I yow forbede ''vp'' peyne of deeth.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Franklin’s Tale, l. 753.}}}}
'''Up a stump, up a tree.''' {{smaller|See ''stump'', ''tree''.}}—'''Up hill and down dale.''' {{smaller|See ''hill''<sup>1</sup>.}}

'''up''' (up), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [< ''up'', ''adv.''] '''I.''' ''a.'' Inclining or tending up; going up; upward: as, an ''up'' grade; an ''up'' train; an ''up'' beat in music; an ''up'' bow in violin-playing.
{{smaller block|No sooner were we on ''up''-grades than I exhausted myself by my vigorous back-pedalling.
{{right|''J. and E. R. Pennell'', Canterbury Pilgrimage on a Tricycle.}}}}
{{smaller|'''Up-bow mark''', in music for the violin, a sign, v, indicating that a note or phrase is to be played with an up bow.}}

'''II.''' ''n.'' Used in the phrase ''ups and downs'', rises and falls; alternate states of prosperity and the contrary; vicissitudes.
{{smaller block|A mixture of a town-hall and an hospital; not to mention the bad choice of the situation in such a country; it is all ''ups'' that should be ''downs''. ''Walpole'', Letters, II. 464.
Every man who has seen the world, and has had his ''ups and downs'' in life, . . . must have frequently experienced the truth of this doctrine. ''Goldsmith'', The Bee, No. 3.
<poem>Life is chequer’d; a patchwork of smiles and of frowns;
We value its ''ups'', let us muse on its ''downs''.</poem>
{{right|''F. Locker'', Piccadilly.}}}}

'''U. P.''' An abbreviation of ''United Presbyterian.''

'''up-and-down''' (up′and-doun′), ''a.'' Plain; direct; unceremonious; downright; positive. Compare ''up and down'', under ''up'', ''adv.'' [Colloq.]
{{smaller block|Miss Debby was a well-preserved, ''up-and-down'', positive, cheery, sprightly maiden lady of an age lying somewhere in the indeterminate region between forty and sixty. ''H. B. Stowe'', Oldtown, p. 291.}}

'''upanishad''' (ö-pan′i-shad), ''n.'' [Skt.] In ''Sanskrit lit.'', a name given to a series of treatises of theosophic and philosophic contents. {{smaller|They are of different dates. They exhibit the earliest attempts of the Hindu mind to penetrate into the mysteries of creation and existence.}}
{{smaller block|An ''upanishad'' is a passage of more philosophic or theosophic character, an excursus into a higher and freer region of thought, away from the details of the ceremonial and their exposition.
{{right|''Whitney'', Amer. Jour. Philol., VII. 1.}}}}

'''upas''' (ū′pas), ''n.'' [= F. ''upas'', < Malay (Java) ''upas'', poison; in the Celebes and Philippine Islands ''ipo'' or ''hipo''.] '''1.''' The poisonous sap of different trees of the Malayan and Philippine Islands, more or less used for arrow-poison. {{smaller|The ''upas-antiar'' is yielded by the antiar or upas-tree. (See def. 2 and ''antiar''.) The ''upas tieuté'', or ''upas radja'', is from the chettik or tjettek, ''Strychnos Tieuté'', one of the strychnine-trees.}}

'''2.''' The tree ''Antiaris toxicaria'', one of the largest Javanese trees, having a cylindrical stem 60 or 70 feet high below the branches. {{smaller|Upon incision a poisonous milky juice flows from the trunk, concreting into a gum, which is mixed with the seed of ''Capsicum frutescens'' and various aromatic substances to form one kind of arrow-poison. The action of the poison is first purgative and emetic, then narcotic, destroying life by tetanic convulsions. Fable invests this tree with a deadly influence upon whatever comes under its branches. It is true that when the tree is felled or the bark extensively wounded it exhales an effluvium producing cutaneous eruptions; otherwise the upas may be approached and ascended like other trees. See ''Antiaris'' and ''sack-tree''.}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
